name: Suvomipic

lead: Suvomipic (PP405) is an experimental scalp gel from Pelage Pharmaceuticals aimed at androgenetic hair loss. People following hair loss research watch it as a possible new regrowth option.

It inhibits the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, which is thought to push dormant follicle stem cells toward glycolysis and growth. In preliminary phase 2a results released in June 2025, 31% of men reached a hair density gain of 20% or more at eight weeks, with no placebo responders; the trial was designed mainly to assess safety.

paras: It is a once-daily topical used in clinical trials only. It is not available outside studies, and phase 3 trials were planned for 2026.
It is investigational and not approved anywhere. Safety data are early-phase and the results come from the company.

chain: Follicle stem cells switch to growth
angle.text: Suvomipic is an experimental once-daily scalp gel that blocks the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, which is thought to switch follicle stem cells toward growth and regrow scalp hair. Company-reported phase 2a results showed density gains at eight weeks.

lead: Suvomipic (developmental code PP405, also JXL069) is an experimental scalp gel for pattern hair loss developed by Pelage Pharmaceuticals, a company spun out of UCLA in 2018.[1] It is applied topically with the aim of reactivating dormant hair follicles in thinning areas, so that hair regrows and the scalp looks denser.[1][2] It is described as a possible first-in-class drug because it works on follicle stem cell metabolism rather than hormones, unlike finasteride and minoxidil.[1]

It is formulated as a 0.05% gel applied once daily, and inhibits the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC1 and MPC2), which raises pyruvate and is thought to increase lactate and glycolysis in follicle stem cells to drive growth.[1] Preliminary phase 2a results released in June 2025 reported that 31% of men with advanced baldness gained 20% or more in hair density at eight weeks, versus none of the placebo group, in a trial mainly designed to assess safety.[1] The drug is not approved anywhere.[1]
Interest in the compound spread to hair-loss forums, where some members discussed obtaining JXL069 from overseas suppliers before approval.[1]

paras: Wikipedia describes accumulation of pyruvate stimulating lactate dehydrogenase in hair follicle stem cells, raising lactate and glycolysis and providing energy for growth.[1] The developers argue that this reactivates dormant follicles by altering stem cell metabolism.[1] Pelage describes it as non-invasive and non-hormonal, based on UCLA scientists' discovery of a metabolic switch that activates follicle stem cells.[2] Wikipedia notes that such a drug is thought to work only if follicles are intact but dormant, and that fibrosis or micro-scarring may limit regeneration.[1]

Topical use was chosen over oral for safety and tolerability, and the drug is reported to be unstable in blood, limiting systemic absorption.[1] The developers say it was engineered to penetrate skin roughly 1,000 times better than blood, and no suvomipic was detected in circulation in clinical studies.[1]

The compound derives from UK-5099, described in 1975.[1] A 2021 Journal of Medicinal Chemistry paper reported synthesis and testing of UK-5099 analogues as MPC inhibitors for hair loss, including JXL069 with a 7-azaindole core, and more than 10 analogues promoted obvious hair growth in shaved mice.[3] Pelage was founded in 2018 by Bill Lowry, Heather Christofk and Michael Jung, received an Allergan option in 2019 that was terminated in 2020, and announced a 120 million dollar Series B in October 2025.[1] Time named it among the best inventions of 2025.[1]

Pelage has said suvomipic is not JXL069, while a July 2026 WHO international nonproprietary name list identifies it as JXL069, an unresolved discrepancy.[1] Members of the r/Tressless community believed JXL069 was suvomipic and sourced it from China in 2025; one sent a sample for lab authentication, and the company does not endorse other use of the compounds.[1]

First human trials began in 2023 in Orange County, California, and phase 1 and phase 2a trials are complete.[1] In the phase 2a results released in June 2025, 31% of men with advanced baldness gained 20% or more in hair density at eight weeks after four weeks of treatment, with no placebo responders; developers said the new hair was thick terminal hair but did not share photos.[1] A three-month open-label extension was completed, with data due in 2026, and phase 3 trials were planned for 2026, with earliest approval estimated at 2027 to 2029.[1] Peer-reviewed full results were not located.

lore.intro: Hair-loss communities discussed JXL069 as a possible early-access version of the Pelage drug.[1]

claims.claim: JXL069 sold online is the same compound as Pelage's PP405
